clips.title: Tanenhaus et al. · One apple
clips.caption: Watch the apple move from its starting towel into the box.
clips.method: The 1995 study used real tabletop objects. This overhead reconstruction preserves the one-apple object set and intended final action. Object appearance, movement timing and the omitted hand are illustrative. It does not show a measured gaze trace or an observed participant recording. The existing studio instruction recording is reused, not claimed as the original experimenter's recording.

clips.title: Tanenhaus et al. · Two apples
clips.caption: The second apple stays on its napkin while the apple on the towel moves into the box.
clips.method: The pencil is replaced by an apple on a napkin, as in the paper's two-referent condition. The same instruction now identifies which apple to move. This is a code-drawn reconstruction of real objects, with illustrative movement timing and no measured gaze data. An early look toward the empty towel is not represented as a required move to that towel.

clips.title: McMurray et al. · Picture selection
clips.caption: Four pictures appear, followed by a central click and an illustrated picture response.
clips.method: Uses Figure 3 as reproduced in the original course slide, not newly drawn substitutes. The initial picture preview lasts 500 ms. The center click starts the listening portion; the later picture click is an illustrative response, not recorded participant data. This preview is silent because the original 0–40 ms Klatt-synthesized tokens have not been recovered and verified. The paper's actual trial included an auditory token and eye tracking. No ordinary word recording has been substituted.

clips.title: Levi & Polat · Line alignment
clips.caption: Watch three one-second presentations of two slightly misaligned, abutting dark lines.
clips.method: The original Vernier task presented two abutting dark lines for one second through a circular aperture, with monocular viewing. Participants rated offsets from −2 to +2 and received feedback. This movie preserves the line geometry and one-second exposure, but enlarges offsets for visibility; screen pixels, luminance, angular size, intertrial pauses, sequence and appearance are illustrative. It is not a calibrated acuity test, an exact oscilloscope simulation, or a recording of the original trials.
